title: Saturn's hexagon
hook: At Saturn's north pole, a jet stream forms a hexagon with sides longer than Earth.
peek: Saturn's north pole is ringed by a jet stream shaped like a near-perfect hexagon, each side wider than our planet. It first showed up in Voyager images from the early 1980s and was still there when Cassini arrived decades later.
lede: Around Saturn's north pole runs a jet stream that does not form a circle. It forms a hexagon, with six fairly straight sides, each longer than Earth is wide. Voyager images taken in the early 1980s revealed it, though it was only noticed in them in 1988, and NASA's Cassini spacecraft, which orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, found it still in place. It is one of the most stable weather patterns known.

bullets.text: At the very centre of the hexagon sits a huge storm with an eye, a little like a hurricane but locked over the pole rather than drifting.
Between 2012 and 2016, Cassini saw the inside of the hexagon turn from bluish to golden. Scientists think haze formed as the north pole moved into summer sunlight.

In 2010 researchers at Oxford spun a tank of water with a faster-turning ring inside. Where the flows met, the fluid formed polygons, including hexagons, suggesting the shape arises naturally from differing wind speeds.
Saturn's south pole has its own swirling storm, but Cassini found no hexagon around it. The six-sided jet stream is a feature of the north alone.
